readerTitle: The day Microsoft's new CEO got it wrong on stage
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Microsoft, 사티아 나델라의 2014년 Grace Hopper 발언과 사과) + 실제 연구 (캐럴 드웩의 마인드셋 연구) + 가상 적용 (물류 창고)
insight: 리더의 성장 마인드셋은 구호가 아니라, 자신이 공개적으로 틀린 순간에 어떻게 행동하는지로 증명된다.
misconception: 리더가 실수를 인정하면 권위를 잃는다. 문화는 새 가치 선언문으로 바뀐다.

sources.text: Microsoft News Center (2014년 2월 4일). 사티아 나델라 CEO 선임 발표
Nadella, S. (2017). Hit Refresh. Harper Business. 'learn-it-all' 개념, 드웩 연구의 영향, Grace Hopper 발언에 대한 회고
2014년 10월 Grace Hopper Celebration 발언과 직원 대상 이메일 보도 (The Verge, GeekWire 등 당시 기사)
Dweck, C. (2006). Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. Random House.
Dweck, C. (2015). Carol Dweck Revisits the 'Growth Mindset'. Education Week. 'false growth mindset' 경고
Microsoft 보도자료: Office for iPad 출시 (2014년 3월), 시가총액 1조 달러 돌파 보도 (2019년 4월)

factChecks.note: Grace Hopper Celebration 발언 시점(2014년 10월)과 내용(임금 인상을 요구하지 말고 시스템을 믿으라는 취지, 'karma' 언급)을 당시 기사로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 요지만 풀어 썼고 직접 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다.
직원 이메일에서 질문에 'completely wrong'하게 답했다고 쓴 부분은 널리 보도된 표현입니다. 이메일 발송 시점(당일인지 다음 날인지)이 불확실해 카드에는 'soon after'로 적었습니다. 동일 노동 동일 임금, 인상이 필요하면 요청하라는 내용도 원문으로 확인하세요.
나델라가 Hit Refresh에서 이 사건을 배움의 계기로 회고했는지, 드웩의 연구를 영향으로 언급했는지 책 본문으로 확인하세요.
2014년 대규모 감원(약 18,000명, 상당수가 Nokia 인수 관련)은 카드에 수치 없이 'large job cuts'로만 적었습니다. 시가총액 1조 달러 돌파는 2019년 4월 기준이며, 문화 변화와의 인과관계는 단정하지 않았습니다.
Microsoft의 이전 문화가 내부 경쟁적이었다는 묘사는 일반적 평가로만 적었습니다. 스택 랭킹 폐지는 나델라 취임 전인 2013년 발표라 나델라의 업적으로 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The day Microsoft's new CEO got it wrong on stage
body: Satya Nadella became Microsoft's CEO in February 2014. He soon began asking staff to stop being *know-it-alls* and become *learn-it-alls*.
A few months later, the man selling that idea gave a badly wrong answer in front of a packed hall. How he handled it did more for his message than any speech.

image.label: A lone speaker on a big stage under a spotlight
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 큰 컨퍼런스 무대 위에 정장 차림 인물 한 명이 스포트라이트를 받으며 서 있고, 객석에는 사람들이 가득함. 무대 위에 작은 말풍선 하나가 금 간 모습. 실제 인물의 얼굴, Microsoft 로고, 행사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You just said the wrong thing in public.
body: You're months into your first CEO job at a famous company. You've been asking staff to admit what they don't know.

At a conference for women in technology, someone asks what women should do if they feel underpaid. You answer that they shouldn't ask for raises, but trust the system to reward them. Criticism arrives fast and loud. What do you do?

options.text: Explain that your words were taken out of context
options.feedback: It protects your image for a day. But staff learn that even the boss who preaches learning defends himself first.

options.text: Post a short apology and move on to your strategy agenda
options.feedback: It ends the news cycle. But a vague apology doesn't show what you actually learned, so it doesn't teach anyone else.

options.text: Say plainly that you were wrong and state what you now believe
options.feedback: It costs you some pride. It turns your own mistake into proof that the learning message is real.

cards.title: "Completely wrong"
body: This happened to Satya Nadella at the Grace Hopper Celebration in October 2014.

Soon after, he emailed all Microsoft employees. He wrote that he had answered the question **completely wrong**. He said men and women should get equal pay for equal work, and that anyone who thinks they deserve a raise should ask for it.
He didn't blame the format, the question or the reporters. He named the error, then named the better view.

cards.title: A learn-it-all mindset, pointed at yourself
body: Nadella has said Carol Dweck's research on mindset shaped his thinking. Dweck found that people who see ability as something you can grow handle setbacks better than people who see it as fixed.
Applied to yourself, a **learn-it-all mindset** means treating your own mistakes as information about what to learn, not as threats to your reputation.
For a leader, the real test isn't a quiet failure. It's being wrong where everyone can see.

image.label: Two paths: a shield labeled 'defend' and a notebook labeled 'learn'
image.brief: 갈림길 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 길 끝에 방패와 "Defend" 라벨, 오른쪽 길 끝에 펼친 노트와 "Learn" 라벨. 가운데에 넘어진 작은 인물이 일어나는 모습. 실제 인물이나 로고 없음.

cards.title: People copy what leaders do when it costs them.
body: Staff hear many slogans. They believe the ones the boss follows under pressure.

If a CEO who preaches learning had defended a bad answer, employees would read the real rule: protect yourself, hide errors. A public correction sent the opposite signal, at a moment when thousands were watching.
Nadella later wrote about the episode in his book *Hit Refresh* as something he learned from, not something he hid.

cards.title: One moment inside a larger shift
body: The same attitude showed up in business choices. Microsoft released Office for the iPad in 2014, embraced open-source software it had once fought, and bet heavily on cloud services.
Microsoft's market value later passed $1 trillion in 2019. Many things drove that, including strategy, timing and markets, not culture alone.
The point isn't that one apology built a giant. It's that a culture of admitting gaps made it easier to change direction.

cards.title: Admitting a mistake is not the same as fixing it.
body: An admission only counts if behavior follows. Culture shows up in who gets hired, promoted and paid, not in one email. Microsoft also made hard calls in this period, including large job cuts in 2014.

And the idea can be misused. Dweck herself has warned about a *false growth mindset*: praising effort or telling staff to "learn" while ignoring real problems. A leader's learning has to start with the leader.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You run a distribution warehouse. Last month you pushed a new picking route system and defended it hard in a team meeting.
Now your shift leads bring data: picking errors are up and some orders are shipping late. Everyone remembers how firmly you backed it. What do you do?

options.text: Give it two more months and tell the team they need to adapt
options.feedback: You avoid a U-turn, but late orders keep piling up. Your leads learn that bringing bad news to you is pointless.

options.text: Tell the team you got it wrong, thank the leads for the data, and fix it with them
options.feedback: You lose a little face and gain a team that will flag problems early. That's worth more than being right last month.

options.text: Quietly switch back to the old routes without saying anything
options.feedback: The errors stop, but the lesson doesn't spread. People notice the silence and conclude mistakes aren't talked about here.

cards.softwareNote: In a software team, this is the founder who loudly backed a feature that users ignore. Saying "I was wrong, here's what the data showed" in the team channel makes it safer for engineers to kill their own weak ideas early.

cards.title: Your own mistakes are your loudest leadership message.
body: People don't learn your values from slogans. They learn them from what you do when you're publicly wrong.
**Try it today:** pick one decision you've defended that the facts no longer support. Tell one person: "I got this wrong. Here's what I learned and what I'll change."
